metadata.title: Godot Shading Language
metadata.lecture_opening_description: Predict, build, and test a visible effect
metadata.audience: Beginning shader programmers in CSYE 7270 and independent Godot learners

beats.narration_text: CSYE seventy-two seventy, Building Virtual Environments. Godot Shading Language. Learn to turn coordinates and material inputs into effects you can predict and test.

shot.visual_intent: Professor Bear portrait, course and exact title visible immediately

show.event: Complete portrait/title card holds for measured narration

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear, for CSYE seventy-two seventy, Building Virtual Environments. Shaders compute from their inputs. Once you can predict those inputs, the language starts to make sense.

qc.sparse_reason: Mandated hesitant writer bookend; the phrase correction carries the idea.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. G P U: the processor doing parallel graphics work. A vertex is a geometry point. A fragment is a candidate contribution to a pixel. A material describes a surface. U V coordinates address a texture.

shot.visual_intent: Definitions arrive in spoken order
shot.motion_claim: Definitions arrive in spoken order

terms.meaning: A candidate contribution to a pixel.
Coordinates used to address a texture.

beats.narration_text: Start with the rendering pipeline. The vertex function works on geometry. Rasterization turns triangles into covered fragments. The fragment function computes surface values. That is our map: inputs, a calculation, then a visible result.

lecture.why: A flat mesh preserves the actual relationship between vertices and coverage; an isometric conveyor obscures it.

shot.visual_intent: Geometry to fragments
shot.motion_claim: Quad corners move, then the triangle fills with fragment cells.

show.event: Quad corners move, then the triangle fills with fragment cells.

beats.narration_text: Godot uses its own shading language, closely related to G L S L. Save it as dot G D shader. Shader type selects the context. Canvas item serves two D; spatial serves three D.

lecture.why: The executed minimal file makes the structure immediately readable.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal shader_type first; then the processor function.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal shader_type first; then the processor function.

show.event: Reveal shader_type first; then the processor function.

props.title: constant.gdshader

beats.narration_text: Other shader contexts include particles, sky, and fog. Not every context exposes the same processor functions or built-ins. Older Godot three tutorials use dot shader files. In Godot, vertex and fragment replace the usual G L S L main entry point.

lecture.why: The real reference gives students the place to check their shader context.

shot.visual_intent: Focus the actual language reference while identifying context-dependent behavior.
shot.motion_claim: Focus the actual language reference while identifying context-dependent behavior.

show.event: Focus the actual language reference while identifying context-dependent behavior.

beats.narration_text: Select a drawable node, open Material, and assign a ShaderMaterial. That material holds a Shader resource. Here the real editor shows our ColorRect with the material attached. Open its shader to edit the program.

lecture.why: A real editor capture exists; it establishes the actual node and material wiring.

shot.visual_intent: Start at the scene tree, then focus the actual Material field.
shot.motion_claim: Start at the scene tree, then focus the actual Material field.

show.event: Start at the scene tree, then focus the actual Material field.

beats.narration_text: This is a complete first shader. Void means the function returns no ordinary value. Instead, it writes COLOR. Four components specify red, green, blue, and opacity. One in the last component means fully opaque.

lecture.why: Students need the exact runnable syntax before inspecting the result.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal COLOR assignment after the function shell.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal COLOR assignment after the function shell.

show.event: Reveal COLOR assignment after the function shell.

props.title: constant.gdshader

beats.narration_text: Every covered fragment receives the same four numbers, so the whole rectangle becomes pink. This output came from Godot. No texture coordinates appear in the calculation, so there is no reason for one part to differ.

lecture.why: Actual pixels verify the executable example without inventing output.

shot.visual_intent: Ring the center, then the edge of the same uniform patch.
shot.motion_claim: Ring the center, then the edge of the same uniform patch.

show.event: Ring the center, then the edge of the same uniform patch.

beats.narration_text: For a three D material, write ALBEDO for the base color. The lighting system uses it along with properties such as roughness and the surface normal. ALBEDO is a three-component vector; opacity has its own output.

lecture.why: Exact tested shader source ties the material outputs to code.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal ALBEDO, then ROUGHNESS; retain the spatial declaration.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal ALBEDO, then ROUGHNESS; retain the spatial declaration.

show.event: Reveal ALBEDO, then ROUGHNESS; retain the spatial declaration.

props.title: spatial.gdshader

beats.narration_text: In a spatial shader, ALPHA controls opacity. This small example writes zero point three. Defining light lets you customize lighting where that processor is supported; you do not need an empty light function in every shader.

lecture.why: The exact program sets up the following real opaque and transparent comparison.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal the independent ALPHA output after ALBEDO.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal the independent ALPHA output after ALBEDO.

show.event: Reveal the independent ALPHA output after ALBEDO.

props.title: alpha.gdshader

beats.narration_text: Here is the rendered cube. Writing ALPHA as zero point three makes a transparent surface. That alone does not create physically convincing glass. Refraction, lighting, and transparency sorting are separate questions.

lecture.why: A paired comparison exposes the limit of the transcript’s glass analogy.

shot.visual_intent: Transparency is not glass
shot.motion_claim: Reveal the opaque render, then the actual alpha render beside it.

show.event: Reveal the opaque render, then the actual alpha render beside it.

beats.narration_text: Coordinates, Not Memory.

shot.visual_intent: Act title arrives and holds
shot.motion_claim: Act title arrives and holds

qc.sparse_reason: Mandated lecture act-title card; single title on cream stage is correct design.

beats.narration_text: Now coordinates. In a two D vertex function, VERTEX gives a local position. Add twenty to its horizontal component and the drawn geometry shifts right. Use twenty point zero because that component is a float.

lecture.why: The exact built-in and floating literal are the teaching target here.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal VERTEX.x and its increment.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal VERTEX.x and its increment.

props.title: vertex.gdshader

beats.narration_text: Before it moves, predict what happens to the collider. The drawn square shifts; the collision outline stays put. A shader changes rendering. It does not move the node or rewrite your physics shape.

lecture.why: The labeled conceptual overlay exposes a distinction a still cannot show.

shot.visual_intent: Rendering versus physics
shot.motion_claim: Hold the initial aligned square and collider, then move only the filled square.

show.event: Hold the initial aligned square and collider, then move only the filled square.

beats.narration_text: TIME is an engine clock. Feeding it into sine makes the offset oscillate. Each frame recomputes the offset from the supplied time. We are not accumulating the previous frame’s vertex position.

lecture.why: The exact expression shows that time is an input rather than stored position.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal amplitude, then the sine expression.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal amplitude, then the sine expression.

show.event: Reveal amplitude, then the sine expression.

props.title: wave.gdshader

beats.narration_text: A clock value of zero, then a quarter turn, then a half turn produces zero offset, maximum offset, then zero again. For an event like damage, drive your own uniform from game state instead of treating TIME as an event timer.

lecture.why: A schematic clock isolates the dependency; captures would confound wall time.

shot.visual_intent: Control the clock
shot.motion_claim: A clock marker advances while one quad shifts and returns.

show.event: A clock marker advances while one quad shifts and returns.

beats.narration_text: UV gives texture coordinates for the current point. This example places U into red and V into green. Blue stays zero. We are turning an invisible coordinate field into something we can inspect.

lecture.why: Runnable color encoding connects the conceptual field to shader syntax.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal UV inside the vec4 constructor.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal UV inside the vec4 constructor.

show.event: Reveal UV inside the vec4 constructor.

props.title: uv.gdshader

beats.narration_text: On this rectangle, the upper left is dark. Move right and red increases. Move down and green increases. The lower right combines both. The gradient is many invocations applying one rule to different inputs.

lecture.why: The actual Godot gradient proves the mapping used by this example.

shot.visual_intent: Camera focuses upper left, then lower right; no camera transition across midpoint.
shot.motion_claim: Camera focuses upper left, then lower right; no camera transition across midpoint.

show.event: Camera focuses upper left, then lower right; no camera transition across midpoint.

beats.narration_text: Do not picture a paintbrush remembering the last pixel. Each fragment has local inputs and local work. Other pixels can be read through appropriate textures, but you cannot rely on the neighboring invocation having already finished.

lecture.why: A grid of actual fragment locations is more direct than a physical factory metaphor.

shot.visual_intent: Independent invocations
shot.motion_claim: All cells receive their own coordinate marker; erase the imagined serial arrow.

show.event: All cells receive their own coordinate marker; erase the imagined serial arrow.

beats.narration_text: Types You Can See.

shot.visual_intent: Act title arrives and holds
shot.motion_claim: Act title arrives and holds

qc.sparse_reason: Mandated lecture act-title card; single title on cream stage is correct design.

beats.narration_text: Types make the calculation explicit. Bool holds true or false. Int holds an integer. Float holds a real-valued approximation. Statements end in semicolons. Convert an integer deliberately when a calculation needs a float.

lecture.why: Exact declarations are the evidence and the usable pattern.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal bool, int, then the explicit float constructor.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal bool, int, then the explicit float constructor.

show.event: Reveal bool, int, then the explicit float constructor.

props.title: scalars.gdshader

beats.narration_text: Here is a deliberate failure: assigning the integer literal five directly to a float. Godot reports a type error. Five point zero or an explicit float conversion fixes it. Read the shader diagnostics, not just the process exit status.

lecture.why: Recorded local diagnostics test the claim rather than merely repeat it.

shot.visual_intent: Show the exact invalid line followed by the actual compiler diagnostic.
shot.motion_claim: Show the exact invalid line followed by the actual compiler diagnostic.

show.event: Show the exact invalid line followed by the actual compiler diagnostic.

props.title: Recorded local evidence · Godot shader lab
lines: SHADER ERROR: Invalid assignment of 'int' to 'float'.

beats.narration_text: A vector groups components. These four numbers can be addressed as X, Y, Z, W, or as red, green, blue, alpha. The names change with your interpretation; the underlying four values do not.

lecture.why: Stable cells make aliasing visible before syntax grows.

shot.visual_intent: Vectors are components
shot.motion_claim: Four fixed cells keep their values while component labels switch.

show.event: Four fixed cells keep their values while component labels switch.

beats.narration_text: Swizzling selects and reorders components. B G R reverses the three color channels. X X copies the first component into a two-component vector. Match the result’s size, and never mix naming families inside one swizzle.

lecture.why: The exact tested forms prevent the transcript’s mistaken vec2/three-component example.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal c.bgr, then c.xx; keep the original vector visible.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal c.bgr, then c.xx; keep the original vector visible.

show.event: Reveal c.bgr, then c.xx; keep the original vector visible.

props.title: swizzle.gdshader

beats.narration_text: A matrix constructor takes columns. Put one and two in the first column, three and four in the second. Multiplying by the first basis vector selects that first column: one, two. It does not select the first row.

lecture.why: The column-versus-row misconception requires spatial arrangement.

shot.visual_intent: Matrices use columns
shot.motion_claim: Two column vectors assemble into a matrix; highlight the first column as output.

show.event: Two column vectors assemble into a matrix; highlight the first column as output.

beats.narration_text: Here is that calculation in shader code. Matrix indexing also starts with the column. The result is divided by four only to fit this color demonstration. The colored output is a diagnostic encoding, not a new matrix rule.

lecture.why: The source distinguishes the mathematical result from its color encoding.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal matrix constructor then matrix-vector multiplication and display scaling.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal matrix constructor then matrix-vector multiplication and display scaling.

show.event: Reveal matrix constructor then matrix-vector multiplication and display scaling.

props.title: matrix.gdshader

beats.narration_text: An array stores several values of the same type. Its first index is zero. These three weights live at indices zero, one, and two. Index one selects zero point three. Keep every access inside the array’s bounds.

lecture.why: Small exact code preserves the declaration and indexing syntax.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal the array, then the weights[1] access.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal the array, then the weights[1] access.

show.event: Reveal the array, then the weights[1] access.

props.title: array.gdshader

shot.visual_intent: Act title arrives and holds
shot.motion_claim: Act title arrives and holds

beats.narration_text: Now make the material adjustable. A uniform supplies a value shared by the invocations using that material. Source color gives a color control; hint range gives a numeric control. The shader reads those values while it runs.

lecture.why: The declarations expose the type, hint, default, and scope without small Inspector text.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal the two uniform declarations before their use.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal the two uniform declarations before their use.

show.event: Reveal the two uniform declarations before their use.

props.title: uniform.gdshader (declarations)

beats.narration_text: An enum hint names integer choices. A range hint guides the Inspector, but it does not enforce a runtime bound. Our local test stored seven in a parameter whose suggested range was zero to one. Clamp when the effect requires it.

lecture.why: Exact source plus captured output separates the editor convenience from runtime validation.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal enum declaration, set_shader_parameter excerpt, then the recorded value.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal enum declaration, set_shader_parameter excerpt, then the recorded value.

show.event: Reveal enum declaration, set_shader_parameter excerpt, then the recorded value.

props.title: uniform.gdshader + lab.gd (excerpts)

beats.narration_text: Predict what happens when two nodes share this ShaderMaterial and we change its tint. Both become orange. The value belongs to the shared material resource, so duplicating a node does not automatically give it independent parameters.

lecture.why: Real output demonstrates the shared-resource consequence more directly than an ownership metaphor.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal both patches, then ring their identical colors.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal both patches, then ring their identical colors.

show.event: Reveal both patches, then ring their identical colors.

beats.narration_text: One fix is a separate material resource. The two materials can still share the same shader program. Here only one tint changes. You need different parameter storage, not another copy of the shader’s source code.

lecture.why: The actual run proves independence; narration supplies the resource relationship.

shot.visual_intent: Move the focus from orange left to blue right.
shot.motion_claim: Move the focus from orange left to blue right.

show.event: Move the focus from orange left to blue right.

beats.narration_text: Another option is an instance uniform, supported for canvas item and spatial shaders in the stable reference checked here. Set it on each drawable node. The material stays shared while the tint varies. Check support in your project’s version.

lecture.why: Literal tested syntax plus setter is the useful distinction.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal instance uniform, then show the node setter excerpt.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal instance uniform, then show the node setter excerpt.

show.event: Reveal instance uniform, then show the node setter excerpt.

props.title: instance.gdshader + lab.gd (excerpts)

beats.narration_text: A sampler binds a texture. Texture reads sample that image at supplied coordinates. Here image tex is the input and UV is the address. Use source color for color textures; a data map has a different role.

lecture.why: Exact sampling syntax is needed before inspecting the captured checkerboard.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal sampler declaration, then texture(image_tex, UV).
shot.motion_claim: Reveal sampler declaration, then texture(image_tex, UV).

show.event: Reveal sampler declaration, then texture(image_tex, UV).

props.title: sampler.gdshader

beats.narration_text: This checkerboard is a real texture sample. On a Sprite, sampling TEXTURE directly reads the texture alone. Incoming COLOR already includes the normal texture and vertex-color contribution. Choose deliberately, or your effect can discard tint and modulation.

lecture.why: The capture establishes sampling; the distinction is carried into the later COLOR-preserving effect.

shot.visual_intent: Zoom to a checker boundary to show that sampling chooses image values.
shot.motion_claim: Zoom to a checker boundary to show that sampling chooses image values.

show.event: Zoom to a checker boundary to show that sampling chooses image values.

beats.narration_text: Passing Values, Choosing Paths.

shot.motion_claim: Act title arrives and holds

beats.narration_text: A varying carries data between stages. Here the vertex function writes horizontal from U. The fragment function reads it. This is stage-to-stage transport, not a variable storing yesterday’s frame or a neighbor’s output.

lecture.why: Exact stage functions expose who writes and reads the value.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal varying declaration, writer, then reader.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal varying declaration, writer, then reader.

show.event: Reveal varying declaration, writer, then reader.

props.title: varying.gdshader

beats.narration_text: The endpoints carry zero and one. Between them, rasterization interpolates the value. Halfway across this flat rectangle, the value is about one half. That is why a few vertex values can create a smooth fragment gradient.

lecture.why: Animation explains where the in-between values come from.

shot.visual_intent: Interpolation between vertices
shot.motion_claim: Two endpoint values persist while an interpolated ramp grows between them.

show.event: Two endpoint values persist while an interpolated ramp grows between them.

beats.narration_text: Ordinary conditionals work inside the shader. This example chooses dark on the left and light on the right by comparing U with one half. The decision is local to each invocation, so different fragments take different branches.

lecture.why: The actual source is small enough to make local control flow explicit.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal the condition before the two branch assignments.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal the condition before the two branch assignments.

show.event: Reveal the condition before the two branch assignments.

props.title: branch.gdshader

beats.narration_text: A switch selects an integer case. Here mode one produces one quarter. Break stops execution from continuing into later cases. Include explicit breaks in the demonstrated version, including the default branch.

lecture.why: The tested syntax matters; this excerpt keeps all cases readable.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal the selected case and its break, then the other cases.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal the selected case and its break, then the other cases.

show.event: Reveal the selected case and its break, then the other cases.

props.title: switch.gdshader (fragment excerpt)

beats.narration_text: Remove the first two breaks and mode one keeps going: one quarter, then three quarters, then one tenth. The captured outputs differ. The language accepted the program; the control flow still changed the meaning.

lecture.why: A trace plus actual rendered difference makes the bug concrete.

shot.visual_intent: Fallthrough changes the result
shot.motion_claim: Trace the three values in order; reveal the two real output patches side by side.

show.event: Trace the three values in order; reveal the two real output patches side by side.

beats.narration_text: A loop needs a clear stopping condition and progress toward it. This one visits three weights, advances its index, and adds them to one. Keeping the bound small also keeps the work per fragment understandable.

lecture.why: Students need a complete working for-loop they can copy safely.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal initialization, bound, increment, then addition.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal initialization, bound, increment, then addition.

show.event: Reveal initialization, bound, increment, then addition.

props.title: loop.gdshader

beats.narration_text: Watch the index: zero, one, two, then stop at three. A while loop also needs progress. A missing increment can hang rendering. We inspect that failure in a trace; we do not freeze the editor to prove it.

lecture.why: A bounded trace teaches the failure without intentionally hanging the GPU.

shot.visual_intent: Termination is part of correctness
shot.motion_claim: Cursor advances through three array cells and lands at a stop marker; missing-progress branch stays unexecuted.

show.event: Cursor advances through three array cells and lands at a stop marker; missing-progress branch stays unexecuted.

beats.narration_text: Build, Verify, Keep Learning.

beats.narration_text: Put the pieces together. Preserve incoming COLOR, blend its RGB toward a tint, and keep its alpha. Clamp the amount between zero and one. That makes the input contract explicit even when game code sends an unexpected value.

lecture.why: The complete tested effect is the reusable student artifact.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal base preservation, mix with clamp, and base.a.
shot.motion_claim: Reveal base preservation, mix with clamp, and base.a.

show.event: Reveal base preservation, mix with clamp, and base.a.

props.title: flash.gdshader

beats.narration_text: Before looking, predict three settings. Zero should preserve the base. One should reach the tint. One half should lie between them. These are the actual rendered samples. Transparent artwork needs a separate alpha check too.

lecture.why: Native Godot output tests the prediction under a stated renderer.

shot.visual_intent: Hold the three labeled settings, then inspect each patch in order.
shot.motion_claim: Hold the three labeled settings, then inspect each patch in order.

show.event: Hold the three labeled settings, then inspect each patch in order.

beats.narration_text: A parser check is useful, but a rendered image answers a different question. Our test inspects shader errors and selected pixels. It does not prove performance on every device or whether this color communicates danger well in your game.

lecture.why: The recorded local report makes the evidence boundary auditable.

shot.visual_intent: Recorded verification lines arrive; separate numerical checks from visual judgment.
shot.motion_claim: Recorded verification lines arrive; separate numerical checks from visual judgment.

show.event: Recorded verification lines arrive; separate numerical checks from visual judgment.

beats.narration_text: Use the stable documentation for first two D and first three D shaders. Then keep the language reference nearby. If you know G L S L, use the migration guide. Match documentation to your installed release.

lecture.why: The live documentation is shown as itself, with exact links in the companion.

shot.visual_intent: Push into the real tutorial heading and introduction.
shot.motion_claim: Push into the real tutorial heading and introduction.

beats.narration_text: The Book of Shaders teaches the mathematical habits: coordinate fields, shaping functions, patterns, and noise. Its examples use plain G L S L. Translate the entry points and inputs into Godot rather than pasting every example unchanged.

lecture.why: The actual resource is recognizable and the transfer limitation is explicit.

shot.visual_intent: Move from the real title to the contents list.
shot.motion_claim: Move from the real title to the contents list.

show.event: Move from the real title to the contents list.

beats.narration_text: Godot Shaders is a community library. Choose a small effect, check its Godot version and license, and change one parameter at a time. Predict the visible difference before running it. Reading a shader is active experimentation.

lecture.why: A real capture avoids inventing library entries or claiming all examples are compatible.

shot.visual_intent: Focus the actual shader gallery after establishing the site.
shot.motion_claim: Focus the actual shader gallery after establishing the site.

show.event: Focus the actual shader gallery after establishing the site.

beats.narration_text: Visual Shaders offer a graph editor for building these programs. Nodes change the authoring interface; they do not remove the need to understand coordinates, types, and data flow. Use the form that helps you inspect the calculation.

lecture.why: The official real interface image keeps the tool recognizable without a fake session.

shot.visual_intent: Camera moves into the real VisualShader documentation and its node-graph example.
shot.motion_claim: Camera moves into the real VisualShader documentation and its node-graph example.

show.event: Camera moves into the real VisualShader documentation and its node-graph example.

beats.narration_text: Compute shaders use raw G L S L through RenderingDevice. They are a separate low-level path for general GPU work. The official tutorial requires a RenderingDevice renderer, such as Forward Plus or Mobile, rather than Compatibility.

lecture.why: The actual prerequisite prevents promising compute in this Compatibility lab.

shot.visual_intent: Focus the actual renderer requirement, then the compute code.
shot.motion_claim: Focus the actual renderer requirement, then the compute code.

show.event: Focus the actual renderer requirement, then the compute code.

beats.narration_text: Keep one loop: predict a visible change, alter one input, run the engine, and compare the result. If the result surprises you, inspect the type, coordinates, and ownership of that input before adding more code.

lecture.why: One persistent surface keeps attention on the controlled experiment rather than an abstract production process.

shot.visual_intent: The experiment loop
shot.motion_claim: A single patch persists through predicted, changed, rendered, and compared states.

show.event: A single patch persists through predicted, changed, rendered, and compared states.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. For CSYE seventy-two seventy, Building Virtual Environments. Choose the shader type and the output for its stage. Compute from coordinates and inputs, not the previous pixel. Match scalar types, vector sizes, and matrix columns. Know whether a value belongs to a material or an instance. Pass varyings deliberately and keep control flow bounded. Predict, render, compare, then judge the effect in context.
